Dear Sarika,
I went back to Hazaribagh last weekend. I know I said I would wait until you could come too, but I needed to see it.
The pond where we raced paper boats is a car park now. Mrs Oraon's mango tree is gone; there's a mobile shop there. Our old house is painted green. A family I didn't know was drying clothes on our terrace.
I stood across the road and felt stupid for crying. It's a good house. They looked happy.
It's not really the house I miss, is it? It's us at eight and ten, Papa coming home on his cycle, you stealing my mangoes. Nothing I can visit.
Next time, let's go together, and then let's go eat chaat somewhere new.
Your sister,
Indu

Mum had made the rajma on the first night, the one we fought over as kids. She kept putting more on our plates.

I was twenty-four, at a construction office. The first Onam, I sat alone in my room and ate bread and jam. I called home and heard everyone laughing around the sadya, and I hung up and stared at the wall.
After that I made two rules. First, every Sunday I called your grandmother. Every Onam I cooked at least three dishes, badly. Second, I said yes to anything my colleagues asked. Cricket with the Pakistani engineers on Fridays. Karaoke with the Filipino accountants. Biryani at Salim's.
By the next Onam, I had eleven people around a sadya on newspaper on my floor. I cried again, but differently.
I'm Darshan, and I'm telling you: carry home, but don't hide inside it.

The whole of Dhanauri had come to the school ground for the district football final. Farhan, fourteen, stood on an upturned crate by the fence with his sister Sharmila.
Their village team was one goal down. Ten minutes left. Farhan's heart thumped so hard he could hear it over the crowd. His fists were clenched. Every time the ball came near the goal, he forgot to breathe.

"Shh!"

Nothing had happened to me. That was the strange part. I'd soaked up the pain of people I'll never meet, and there wasn't one thing I could do for any of them.

Counselling centre note, Friday.
Gopika, nineteen, second year, came in today with her friend Vaibhav, who waited outside. She said she has felt "heavy and on edge" since Sunday but "nothing is wrong". Sleeping late. Snapping at her roommate.
When I asked what she'd been doing in the evenings, she said she'd been following the earthquake news. Videos, rescue clips, families searching. Three or four hours a night. She had no family there and knew no one affected.
She said, "I feel stupid. It's not even my pain."
I told her that feeling others' pain is a sign of care, not stupidity, and that it can soak in when we can't do anything.
What I did next: we made a small plan — news once a day, not at night, and she chose one relief fund her college was collecting for. She'll come back Tuesday.

I'm Arohi, and I shared an office with Amandeep at the helpline for a year. Here's what I noticed.
Some calls were really heavy. A mother whose son hadn't come home. A student who'd lost a friend. After those calls, Amandeep would sit very still for a few seconds, hand flat on the desk. Once I heard Amandeep murmur, "This is hers. Not mine."
Then Amandeep would take off the headset and go for a ten-minute walk round the building, no phone. Every time.
And later, almost always, a small action: an extra shift, a list of local support numbers typed up for a caller, a note to the team about a case.
I asked once how Amandeep didn't carry it all home. "I carry it into the next thing I can do," Amandeep said. "Not into my bed."

Dilnaz, you asked how I lasted thirty years as a reporter without breaking. Let me tell you about my first big story.
I was twenty-five. A bus had gone into a canal near Ropar. I spent three days with the families. I came home and couldn't stop crying. For two weeks I ate standing up, slept in my clothes, read every report again and again.
My editor, an old man named Sethi, called me in. "Baljeet, you're drowning in their sorrow. That helps no one." He told me three things. Say: this is their grief, not mine. Step away from it every evening. And do one useful thing with it.
So I wrote a follow-up about the broken railing. It got fixed. And I started walking by the river each night without a notebook.
That's how I lasted. Not by feeling less. By carrying it differently.

qa.a: Near Ropar.

qa.a: Sethi's advice was the turning point; naming the grief as the families', stepping away each evening and writing about the railing turned the feeling into help.

qa.a: They might have felt a little comforted that something good came from their loss and that someone kept caring.
